analysis.one_liner: Requires extra licensed crews, double hulls, funded oil-spill cleanup plans, and higher tanker liability after the Exxon Valdez spill.
analysis.headline: A Senate committee-approved bill to tighten tanker crewing, spill response, and liability after the Exxon Valdez disaster never got a floor vote; the Senate indefinitely postponed it by unanimous consent on August 2, 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: Written in response to the March 1989 Exxon Valdez spill in Prince William Sound, this bill would have required oil tankers in U.S. waters to carry additional licensed officers and lookouts on the bridge, undergo random and post-accident alcohol testing of crew, install double hulls on newly built tankers, and file and pay for approved oil-spill contingency plans with cleanup equipment pre-positioned near their routes. It would also have required Alaska-licensed pilots for tankers entering and leaving Valdez, a navigation light on Bligh Reef, and it would have raised the liability cap on the Trans-Alaska Pipeline Liability Fund from $100 million to $750 million.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, fish, and work along U.S. coasts, especially Alaska communities whose fisheries and livelihoods were damaged by the Exxon Valdez spill. Stronger crewing, pilot, and spill-response rules would lower the chance of another spill and the damage it causes, and the disaster-assistance change would make federal relief available after a spill. Taxpayers also benefit when shippers, not the public, bear more cleanup and damage costs.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every affected oil tanker transiting pilotage waters to carry an extra deck officer and lookout on the bridge, a second licensed first-class pilot aboard, and a chart position fix at least every six minutes.

Requires periodic, random, and post-accident alcohol testing of tanker crew performing safety-sensitive functions, and lets the Coast Guard check mariners' motor-vehicle driving records and suspend the credentials of those with impaired-driving records.
Requires newly constructed oil tankers to be equipped with double hulls and double bottoms through a rulemaking due within one year.

Requires tanker owners to submit government-approved oil-spill contingency plans, pre-position cleanup equipment and trained personnel sufficient for the maximum probable spill, drill twice a year, and bars tankers from operating without an approved plan.

For Prince William Sound specifically, requires Alaska-licensed pilots for tankers north of Bligh Reef, a navigation light on Bligh Reef, expanded radar tracking with alarms in the Valdez vessel traffic system, and a Prince William Sound Oil Spill Recovery Institute funded at about $25 million from the pipeline liability fund.

Raises the strict liability cap on the Trans-Alaska Pipeline Liability Fund from $100 million to $750 million, raises vessel-owner liability from $14 million to $70 million, and requires the fund to immediately deposit $150 million for cleanup after an incident.
Amends the Stafford Act so an oil spill qualifies as a major disaster for federal disaster assistance purposes.

analysis.who_pays: Oil tanker owners and operators, who would bear the cost of extra crew, double hulls on new ships, alcohol-testing programs, pre-positioned cleanup equipment, and civil and criminal penalties for violations, and the Trans-Alaska Pipeline Liability Fund, financed by charges on oil moved through the pipeline, whose exposure would rise sevenfold. Some of these costs would be passed through to the price of shipping oil.

drawbacks.text: Most of the bill's key requirements go through rulemaking with explicit waiver authority: the Secretary may waive or modify the crewing, double-hull, and contingency-plan requirements to the extent they are determined not to enhance safety, leaving room for the rules to be diluted in practice.

Several headline items are studies rather than mandates — the bill only requires a proceeding to decide whether electronic position-reporting equipment should be required, and a report on whether tanker sizes should be limited.
Compliance costs for tanker owners, including double hulls and pre-positioned response equipment, would be substantial for new ships and would partly show up in the cost of moving oil.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety payoff is real and the record behind it is concrete: the Exxon Valdez ran aground with a single hull, an over-worked bridge watch, and an officer with a drunk-driving record, and the spill cost far more than the preventive measures this bill requires. The bill's weakness is design: it delegates nearly everything to rulemaking with explicit waiver authority, so its strength depends on how the Coast Guard writes the rules. The costs fall on a concentrated industry and would be modest per barrel relative to the damage one spill can do.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee wrote and reported the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar, but it sat there for a year and on August 2, 1990 the Senate indefinitely postponed it by unanimous consent — no senator ever had to cast a recorded vote on it.

narrative.text: The Senate Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported as an original measure on June 20, 1989, and Senator Hollings reported it to the Senate with written report 101-99 on August 1, 1989, along with additional views filed by one or more committee members.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 196, on August 1, 1989, and attracted no cosponsors.
It sat on the calendar for about a year, until August 2, 1990, when the Senate indefinitely postponed it by unanimous consent, removing it from consideration without any recorded vote on its merits.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tanker owners and oil shippers were better off in the short run, avoiding the crewing, double-hull, and expanded-liability costs this bill would have imposed. For the public the loss was partly temporary: later in the same Congress, Congress enacted broader oil-spill legislation, the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, which imposed similar double-hull and liability requirements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tanker owners, until the 1990 oil-spill law

against.name: Oil shipping and petroleum industry
against.role: Tanker owners, operators, and oil producers affected by the rules
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory double hulls, expanded spill liability, and stricter crewing mandates during the tanker-safety debate that followed the Exxon Valdez spill.

sides.party_line_note: No recorded vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested; the bill was a Democratic chairman's committee product, carried no cosponsors, and was shelved by unanimous consent with additional views filed by some committee members.

industries.note: The bill requires extra licensed bridge crews, alcohol testing, double hulls on newly built tankers, government-approved spill plans with pre-positioned cleanup equipment, entry bans and penalties for violators, and raises vessel-owner liability from $14 million to $70 million. These are exactly the costs that fall on coastal communities when prevention fails.

Raises the Trans-Alaska Pipeline Liability Fund's strict liability cap from $100 million to $750 million, raises vessel-owner liability to $70 million, and requires an immediate $150 million deposit for cleanup after an incident. The fund is financed by charges on oil shipped through the pipeline, so the cost lands on producers and shippers.

industries.industry: Oil spill cleanup and response industry
industries.note: Mandatory contingency plans, pre-positioned booms, skimmers and escort vessels, twice-yearly drills, and a public inventory of response equipment create steady demand for cleanup contractors and equipment, including Coast Guard spill-response contracting.

Mandatory extra deck officers and a second licensed pilot aboard each tanker create licensed crew positions, but random alcohol testing, driving-record checks through the National Driver Register, and on-the-spot license suspension give the government new power over individual mariners.
